What a Derivative Retains

From side strips and oriented boundaries to infinitesimal geometry

Explicit calculations in calculus, algebraic geometry, formal deformation theory, and homotopy theory.

Henry Shin

PDF · 39 pagesMarkdown manuscript

Begin with calculus, polynomial rings, and oriented boundaries. Later sections introduce complexes and homology, then use formal deformation theory, spectra, and homotopy functors.

Ways through this exposition

Ways through the exposition:

From calculus to infinitesimal points: §§1–5. Follow strips, boundaries, and the diagonal to the familiar derivative.

Arithmetic and invisible directions: §§6–7. Change the coefficients and see what first-order measurements detect.

Equations, intersections, and higher operations: §§8–11. Retain a constraint, test its lifts, and recover its nonlinear equation.

Spectra and functors of spaces: §§12–13. Follow coherent multiplication and gluing into two homotopical calculi.

Contents · 14 sections

An expanding rectangle and an oriented square give two pictures of a product rule. One separates a linear change from a quadratic corner; the other separates boundary faces and cancels their endpoints. Following these pictures leads to derivatives over arithmetic rings, defining constraints in cotangent complexes, and nonlinear interactions in homotopy theory.

The organizing question is what a first-order description retains. A scalar slope, a cotangent module, a derived fiber, and a formal deformation law retain different information. Each enlargement below is introduced by a calculation in which that difference matters. Two operations guide the route: discard products of changes to extract a linear response; retain degrees and signs to organize how pieces fit together.

The opening pictures return at the advanced steps. Fixing the rectangle's area turns the strips into a linear constraint and the corner into a possible obstruction. Higher brackets encode the rule producing that obstruction. Spectral differentiation keeps the homotopies in multiplication and in its infinitesimal responses. Goodwillie calculus applies linear approximation to gluing spaces, where a product-cell boundary exhibits the interaction that stabilization loses. These constructions enrich different parts of the original picture; their coefficient choices and reconstruction hypotheses will be stated at each step.

The opening uses calculus and elementary chains. Polynomial algebras and modules enter next; complexes and derived tensor products are introduced when ordinary quotients lose constraints. The final four sections assume familiarity with graded algebra and homotopy theory; the spectral section uses stable homotopy theory. Cohomological complexes use the convention that , for a vector space in degree zero, lies in degree .

1 · The side strips of a rectangle

A rectangle has side lengths and , so its area is . Change the lengths to and . The new area is exactly

For positive increments, the three added pieces are two side strips and a corner: a strip of area , another of area , and a corner of area . The identity also holds for signed increments, with the appropriate removals of area. Dividing the change by gives

The limit retains the strips and discards the corner. This is already a precise answer to what a derivative keeps: the part of the change that scales linearly with the parameter.

The same calculation gives the product rule without assuming that the sides move at constant speeds. If and are differentiable at , put and . Then

The rectangle supplies more than a mnemonic. Its exact decomposition identifies the term that must disappear when we retain only first-order variation. Later, an algebraic infinitesimal will make that disappearance an exact quotient operation.

For example, start with side lengths and , and let both increase by . The area changes from to . At , the added area is : the strips contribute and the corner . The derivative with respect to this common parameter is . It depends on the chosen motion of the two sides. Allowing separate increments instead gives the differential , which can be evaluated on any such motion.

2 · The oriented boundary of the square

Now keep a rectangle fixed and ask how its boundary pieces fit together. Write it as , with , , , and ; these letters now denote endpoints rather than the side lengths above. Orient both intervals in the increasing direction, and orient by the order of the coordinates. The boundary of an interval is its final endpoint minus its initial endpoint:

The square has the counterclockwise boundary

The first term gives the right edge upward and the left edge downward. The second gives the top edge leftward and the bottom edge rightward. The minus sign is the orientation change required when the boundary operation passes the first interval. For oriented cubical chains, the general product formula is

Here the degree of a chain is its dimension.

Apply the boundary once more. Writing here for the vertex at coordinates , the eight endpoint contributions are

Every corner occurs twice, with opposite signs. The statement records this cancellation, including its orientation data. If we retained only the unsigned set of edges and then took their endpoints, we would see four corners. Chains preserve the signs that make the second boundary vanish.

The product rule for slopes and the product rule for boundaries thus share a structural feature: act on one factor at a time. The boundary carries an additional degree and its associated sign. Keeping that degree will matter when products become tensor products of complexes.

The cancellation also explains why a boundary has no boundary as a chain even when individual boundary pieces have endpoints. A right edge alone has two endpoints. Within the whole oriented square, its upper endpoint cancels the initial contribution from the top edge, and its lower endpoint cancels the terminal contribution from the bottom. The identity concerns how the pieces fit together. It is precisely this information that an unsigned picture suppresses.

8 · The cotangent complex retains the equations

The cotangent calculation reads the same constraint backward. In the ambient polynomial algebra , the relation has differential

For , this expression must become zero, giving

Kähler differentials take the cokernel of the map that sends the defining equation to its differential. The cotangent complex retains that map as well:

The symbol records the equation's role. It lies in degree ; the coordinate differentials lie in degree zero. The polynomial is a non-zero-divisor in , so this is the full cotangent complex. Its two free terms can be restricted to by evaluating their coefficients. Dualizing gives

The kernel is the allowed linear motion. The cokernel records constraint violations that a correction of the coordinates cannot remove. Calling it an obstruction target still leaves a calculation to do: we must determine the violation produced at the next order.

The degrees here specify roles, rather than Taylor orders. An equation stays in degree whether it is quadratic or cubic. The resemblance to the boundary complex is the use of degrees and a square-zero differential to organize compatibility. The geometric boundary , the ordinary polynomial derivative, and the differential inside this complex act on different objects.

Moving the embeddings gives a geometric check. A line in meets a distinct line in one point, so moving one copy of produces the count . A fiber is disjoint from when , so moving one copy of produces the count . Before moving, each copy overlaps itself everywhere. The virtual classes retain the intersection information compatible with those motions. Their numbers measure intersection classes, rather than the number of points in the literal overlapping sets.

Classical intersection theory already computes these numbers through normal bundles and refined intersections. Derived geometry retains that information in the intersection object itself. The example also identifies what a pointwise derivative loses: identical intrinsic spaces and identical tangent-complex dimensions can have different global normal geometry. Retaining the conormal bundle makes the intersection count compatible with the geometry of the embedding.

11 · Higher operations distinguish identical tangent complexes

The intersection example recovered how infinitesimal data vary along a curve. A further question concerns the nonlinear law at a single point. Return to the node . Its second-order residual was the rectangle's corner: moving by produced . The first-order tangent complex retained two directions and one obstruction component. To recover the condition that a motion must satisfy, we also needed the rule that combines those directions into . Higher brackets record such interactions.

Polarizing the corner

Work over a field of characteristic zero. The node's quadratic expression is . We can recover its bilinear interaction by applying two displacements, and , and subtracting their separate effects:

These are the two mixed corners: the first displacement's horizontal change combines with the second's vertical change, and vice versa. The expression is linear in each displacement separately. Conversely,

because putting the same displacement in both slots counts its corner twice. This recovery of a homogeneous polynomial from a multilinear operation is called polarization.

We can put this calculation directly on a graded space. Let the two tangent inputs have degree , and let an obstruction generator have degree :

Give it zero linear differential and a binary bracket with

The bracket is graded antisymmetric: exchanging homogeneous inputs contributes . Thus these odd-degree inputs have a symmetric bracket, exactly as the polarized expression requires. Set all higher brackets and every bracket involving to zero. The output component then records a residual of the equation, while the two input components record the displacements that can create it.

For coefficients in the maximal ideal of a local Artin -algebra with residue field , put . The compatibility equation in this binary model, called the Maurer–Cartan equation, is

Taking and recovers the earlier test: the equation vanishes modulo , and its residual modulo is . The bracket consumes two tangent inputs and produces precisely the obstruction that the rectangle calculation identified.

After shifting by , the degree-one inputs become the degree-zero tangent directions, and the degree-two output becomes the degree-one obstruction component. This is exactly the node's two-term tangent complex. Its zero differential records the vanishing Jacobian at the origin, so every direction is allowed by the linear test. The bracket then distinguishes the directions: either axis alone has zero self-bracket, while a mixture has the residual . A two-term space with no operations would leave this distinction unspecified. The multilinear response supplies the missing law, and the compatibility equation applies that law to the proposed motion.

The number of inputs and the homological degree answer different questions. Every has degree , so degree-one inputs still produce a degree-two output. Increasing the arity does not create a new obstruction degree. Higher jets instead increase which powers of a displacement the test algebra retains. Here the graded space has a tangent component and an obstruction component; its operations specify the nonlinear law between them.

In general, the higher identities constrain how the linear differential and several brackets compose. The central-output pattern used here is special: arbitrary formal deformation problems can require nonzero nested operations as well.

Reconstructing the formal equation

The completed Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra makes reconstruction explicit. With the sign of the dual relation generator chosen accordingly, it is

Its degree-zero cohomology is . Its negative cohomology vanishes because multiplication by in is injective. The algebra is consequently a resolution of the actual formal neighborhood. The linear differential of is zero in every case; the different higher brackets reconstruct the different equations.

The shift also matches the earlier calculation: the tangent complex is , putting in degree and in degree . Forgetting the higher brackets leaves precisely the two-component complex shared by the square and cube. Retaining the brackets tells us which polynomial equation connects its components. On derived Artin test algebras, the correspondence includes the homotopies of the deformation space as well as its ordinary solutions.

Characteristic-zero formal moduli theory turns this example into a general principle. The tests are augmented connective derived Artin -algebras with finite-dimensional total homotopy and residue field . A formal moduli problem assigns spaces to these tests, takes to a contractible space, and preserves homotopy pullbacks whenever at least one map into the common target is surjective on . Over a characteristic-zero field, such problems are equivalent to differential graded Lie models, or models, with their full homotopy structure. Their underlying shifted tangent complexes supply the linear data; their operations retain the nonlinear compatibility conditions.

12 · Spectral differentiation and calculations in K theory

The higher brackets retained nonlinear laws over a characteristic-zero field. We now enlarge the coefficient objects so that multiplication and its infinitesimal responses can carry stable homotopy information. The same rectangle calculation still controls first order: in an ordinary square-zero extension, the generator can move to , and the product rule gives

There are possible positions for the one changed factor; every term containing two changed factors vanishes. This is the same strip calculation, iterated through a product of factors. A derivative of a free polynomial algebra is therefore determined by the response of its generator.

In spectral algebra, multiplication comes with coherent homotopies and the coefficients form spectra. A spectrum records compatible information across degrees, including stable homotopy groups. The square-zero interpretation still works. Its universal measurement must now retain families of derivations and homotopies between them, as well as their individual values.

Let be a map of -ring spectra and an -module spectrum. Form the square-zero extension . Define the space of -derivations by

A point is a lift of the identity of ; the space also records homotopies between lifts. The spectral cotangent complex represents this space:

Thus the derivative is an -module spectrum, and its coefficients must be -module spectra. Its homotopy groups yield topological André–Quillen homology, usually abbreviated TAQ.

The coefficient condition has content. Multiplication by an invertible element of must act invertibly on every -module. For example, the degree-two Bott element of forces its modules to be periodic. A nonzero coefficient spectrum with homotopy concentrated in degree zero cannot simply be substituted into a -linear derivation problem. The choice of linear measurements already incorporates part of the algebra being differentiated.

The free example and its families of responses

For a free algebra , the formula is particularly direct:

A derivation is determined by its value on the generating module . The free adjunction identifies lifts into with lifts of , whose space is ; extension of scalars gives the displayed representing object.

For one generator , this says , the spectral version of the free rank-one module . More explicitly,

Here extracts the underlying infinite loop space of a spectrum. Its points give values for the generator's response, and its homotopy groups give higher families of responses. For an ordinary ring , write for its Eilenberg–Mac Lane ring spectrum: , and its other homotopy groups vanish. With , the degree-zero calculation on polynomial functions is exactly the displayed formula .

The free algebra itself remembers a difference that ordinary polynomial notation can conceal:

For and in degree zero, positive homology of the finite symmetric groups vanishes, and this algebra is . For and in degree zero, its weight-two summand contains

This small homology group can be calculated using boundaries. The transposition group is , and its classifying space is . This space has one cell in each dimension. Its positive-dimensional integral cellular differentials alternate between multiplication by and zero. With coefficients, they all become zero:

The one-cell survives in homology, giving . With rational coefficients, the map from degree two to degree one is multiplication by , so that particular class is a boundary.

The free spectral algebra consequently has positive homotopy that lacks. The extra information comes from making permutations of factors compatible through homotopies. It is different from retaining a higher power in a Taylor expansion. The spectral cotangent construction and the cotangent complex of simplicial commutative algebras generally differ in positive characteristic. Rationally the comparison behaves much more simply.

The rectangle becomes a change of orientation

The decisive square-zero calculation is a version of the opening rectangle with both unchanged sides equal to one:

The product of the two changes is the missing corner. Units that reduce to one therefore form an additive infinite loop space, denoted . Spectrally, this space is , including its coherent addition and homotopies.

To see why this calculation brings K-theory into the derivative of complex cobordism, we need the construction of a Thom algebra. Let be an -ring spectrum. The space classifies invertible -module spectra: spectral analogues of one-dimensional lines. A map of grouplike -spaces

specifies a coherently multiplicative family of such lines. Combining labels in tensors their lines. The Thom algebra is their multiplicative colimit. An -orientation is a compatible trivialization of all these lines after extending coefficients to . The identity map of the Thom algebra supplies a canonical reference orientation.

The familiar Thom-class notation suggests the compatibility: . Change the reference trivialization by a unit . The square-zero calculation then reads

These formulas describe relative changes of trivializations; the notation suppresses the line identifications. We require compatibility through all the homotopies, not just this equality of individual Thom classes. An infinitesimal change of multiplicative orientation is consequently an additive, coherently compatible measurement of the labeling family.

The universal property of the Thom algebra makes this statement precise. Lifts of its identity to are lifts of the reference orientation. The zero section supplies a reference lift, and the relative changes from it are maps of -groups to . Hence

Here is the connective spectrum associated to the infinite loop group , with . It is not the ordinary suspension spectrum of the underlying space. If is nonconnective, its additive infinite loop space corresponds to ; mapping spaces from the connective spectrum into this cover and into agree. The final equivalence is extension of scalars from spectra to -modules.

We have thus identified the representing module:

This is the Thom cotangent theorem. The deep input is the Thom algebra's universal orientation property; the square-zero strip calculation explains why its answer is additive and why the labeling spectrum occurs.

Why the labeling spectrum for MU is shifted K-theory

Finite complex vector bundles combine by direct sum. Group completion permits formal differences of bundles and gives ; the integer records virtual rank. Connective complex K-theory is the spectrum associated to this full group completion. The complex J-map associates to a bundle its fiberwise one-point-compactified sphere; virtual subtraction becomes inversion of this sphere family. Complex cobordism , however, is the Thom algebra of the complex -map on the rank-zero family . Removing rank gives

The notation means the cover with homotopy below degree two removed. The rank map is an isomorphism on , and . Bott periodicity supplies the remaining calculation:

Multiplication by the degree-two Bott element is an isomorphism in every degree at least two. Its source has no homotopy in lower degrees, so it identifies with the rank-zero cover. Thus the associated spectrum is , and the Thom formula gives

For any -module , equivalently,

K-theory appears because it is the additive stable theory of the bundles labeling the Thom construction. The derivative measures coherent first-order changes of their orientations. The double suspension records the removal of virtual rank.

A small check makes the spectral contribution visible:

The last equality uses connectivity and the lowest-degree tensor product . The isolated zeroth-ring map is , whose ordinary relative differential is zero. Its degree-zero description misses this degree-two response. Higher integral degrees require a genuine smash-product calculation; one cannot simply tensor all homotopy groups.

KU begins with tensoring lines and then inverts Bott

The second row describes . Periodic is obtained from it by Bott localization, which extends the cotangent's coefficients. The factorial homology calculation below explains why the resulting cotangent module is rational.

For periodic complex K-theory, the result is

Why does the linear response become rational when itself has integral homotopy? Start with another bundle family. The space classifies complex line bundles, with multiplication given by tensor product. This differs from the direct sum on . In degree-zero K-theory the same tensor operation gives the rectangle-like law

At first order its corner disappears. In ordinary cohomology its first Chern class is exactly additive:

This exact additivity will let us calculate the multiplication in homology.

The structured Snaith theorem presents as

Inverting a class introduces no independent first-order choice. The ordinary inverse calculation already suggests the reason:

The response of the inverse is forced by the response of the original class. The spectral localization theorem makes this precise, including coherent lifts: , and extension of coefficients gives

This step retains an integral Eilenberg–Mac Lane spectrum. We still need to explain where the rationals enter.

The explicit factorial calculation

This is the Pontryagin product on homology, rather than the cup product on cohomology or the product on . The ring with this basis and multiplication is the divided-power ring , where . The binomial coefficients count choices of factors, as in the opening strip calculation. They remain visible after passing from line-bundle multiplication to its homological record.

Ordinary integral homology of a spectrum is . Choose the orientation of so that the Hurewicz image of Bott is . Smashing the Snaith presentation with commutes with localization. The graded localization theorem therefore gives

One can also see the denominators forming step by step. Localization is the telescope . After smashing with , its degree-zero groups are

This new telescope explains the arithmetic created by localization. Every even degree has the same eventual factorial progression, and every odd degree is zero. Rationality and periodicity do different jobs

The coefficient-change map sends each to the same class with rational coefficients. After Bott localization it is an isomorphism on the computed Laurent-polynomial homotopy rings. Therefore the specific map

is an equivalence of -modules. Combining this rationalization with the cotangent formula and then Bott periodicity gives

The last equivalence is multiplication by Bott as a module map. Factorial localization produces rationality; Bott then removes the two-degree shift. Periodicity by itself does not force rational coefficients.

The resulting comparison of graded homotopy modules is explicit:

The second Laurent expression describes a module over ; no multiplication on the cotangent complex is being asserted. Thus the cotangent has in every even integer degree and zero in odd degrees. If denotes the degree-two generator in the intermediate module , then has degree zero. This explains how a degree-two labeling spectrum contributes a nonzero degree-zero spectral differential. Looking only at the map , namely , would give a zero ordinary relative cotangent.

There is also a crucial distinction between coefficients and restriction of scalars. The expression above computes ordinary integral homology. The rank map kills Bott and cannot extend to a map , since an invertible class cannot map to zero. Tensoring over would instead give . The absolute smash used in the calculation retains until its inversion forces the factorial denominators.

The signed boundary rule returns in THH

Topological Hochschild homology (THH) is the geometric realization of the cyclic bar construction of a ring spectrum, which organizes iterated smash products using multiplication, unit maps, and cyclic permutation. In this case the differential participates in a complete Hochschild calculation:

This is a proved calculation for . To understand its final simplification, write for the degree-one rational generator. The graded exchange rule gives

It is the same sign principle that makes differential one-forms anticommute and governs the oriented product boundary. In each tensor power of weight , a transposition acts by minus one before taking homotopy orbits. Rational finite-group homology vanishes in positive degrees, and these sign coinvariants vanish as well. All those symmetric-power summands disappear, leaving the square-zero odd summand .

Thus has integral homotopy in even degrees and rational homotopy in odd degrees. Its algebra calculation combines the rectangle's square-zero response, the factorial arithmetic of tensoring lines, and the boundary's graded signs. The comparison with a free algebra on the suspended cotangent is established here by Stonek's theorem; it cannot simply be deduced from a connective Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg theorem, since is nonconnective.

13 · Goodwillie derivatives recover interactions between spaces

The spectral section linearized multiplication and measured its compatible infinitesimal responses. We now let the input itself be a space and ask how a functor responds when spaces are glued together. Return to the rectangle's corner: we can isolate an interaction by comparing a simultaneous change with the two separate changes. For a scalar function, the mixed difference is

If , expansion gives . For a linear function it is zero. The subtraction removes the base value and both separate responses, leaving their interaction.

For the two-variable area function , the corresponding calculation is

This is exactly the corner area. It is a useful starting point for Goodwillie calculus: combine two changes, remove the effects already present separately, and retain what requires both.

The factor of two in the square example counts two ordered mixed choices in its product expansion. The area example specifies a change in each distinct factor and isolates one corner. In both calculations, an interaction is invisible to a description that adds only the separate first-order responses.

The square of spaces

Now the inputs and outputs are based spaces, and is a functor preserving homotopy equivalences. The wedge combines two spaces at their basepoint. Collapsing either summand gives the comparison square

Spaces cannot be subtracted like numbers. Instead, compare the response to the combined input with the homotopy pullback of the separate responses:

This total homotopy fiber is the second cross-effect. A homotopy fiber records a point in the combined response together with the compatible paths making its separate responses trivial. It retains the residual interaction with its homotopies. When is reduced, meaning , the comparison target is .

The exact linearity condition is 1-excision: every homotopy pushout square must become a homotopy pullback square. This requires the absence of a residual interaction for every such gluing test; the wedge comparison is one instance, rather than the entire definition. For higher order, is -excisive when it takes every strongly homotopy cocartesian -cube to a homotopy cartesian cube. “Strongly cocartesian” means each two-dimensional face is a homotopy pushout. “Cartesian” means the initial vertex agrees with the homotopy limit of the remaining vertices.

For suitable homotopy functors, including the identity used below, Goodwillie constructs a universal -excisive approximation . These approximations fit into the tower

The layers retain the successive interactions, as homogeneous terms do in a Taylor expansion.

The diagonal reappears in linearization

There is a precise connection with the cotangent construction. For a map of -ring spectra, form the augmented commutative -algebra . Its first-factor unit and multiplication give , whose composite is the identity. Let be the functor taking an augmented algebra to the homotopy fiber of its augmentation, as an -module. Here measures separation between the two algebra copies before linearization.

The first excisive approximation of this functor gives

Here the gluing tests are pushouts in the category of augmented commutative -algebras, whose zero object is . This theorem is the spectral counterpart of the earlier diagonal construction : linearize the separation data while retaining homotopies. It is an approximation of a functor in that category, rather than a naive quotient of an ordinary ideal. The next calculation applies the same excision principle to the identity functor on based spaces.

Why the first approximation is linear

For the identity functor on based spaces, the first approximation is

The suspension spectrum places in stable homotopy theory, and reads a space from the resulting spectrum. Its first derivative at the one-point space is the sphere spectrum. The reason this approximation removes mixed wedge behavior is visible in the calculation

Finite sums and products agree for spectra. Since preserves products, . The gluing square is handled linearly, and its associated collapse comparison has no mixed fiber. The unstable identity has cross-effect

which can be nontrivial.

The same construction handles general pushouts. The suspension-spectrum functor preserves them; in a stable category every pushout square is also a pullback square; and preserves pullbacks. These three properties explain why satisfies 1-excision, beyond this particular wedge calculation.

The two squares have different maps. The wedge pushout has vertices and inclusion maps; its image under has vertices and is a homotopy pullback. The cross-effect square instead uses collapse maps to compare the combined response with the separate responses. The general pushout argument and the explicit product calculation show that passes both tests.

The boundary that attaches the product cell

The opening boundary picture now gives a concrete interaction. Take and . Choose characteristic maps that collapse to the basepoint. The product of the two disks is a four-dimensional cell, with boundary

The two boundary pieces meet in the torus . Define a map as follows. On , send to in the second sphere. On , send it to in the first sphere. Both descriptions send the common torus to the wedge point, so they glue.

This is a decomposition of a boundary into spaces and maps. Its orientations are governed by the same chain product rule used for the square. The induced boundaries of the two pieces are respectively and ; their common boundary cancels as a chain. The union itself is not a subtraction of homotopy types.

With a choice of product orientation and characteristic maps, represents the mixed Whitehead product, up to the corresponding overall sign:

Attaching the four-cell along turns into . The map retains how the two spheres interact before that cell fills the interaction.

The four-cell also explains why this class belongs to the cross-effect. Composing with gives the boundary restriction of the product map . That map extends over the whole product of disks. It supplies a nullhomotopy in the product, so , together with that nullhomotopy, lifts to the homotopy fiber. Its two separate projections lose the interaction, while the fiber retains it.

Its effect is substantial:

The Hopf maps , supported on the individual spheres, stabilize modulo two. The mixed Whitehead product vanishes after suspension. The first approximation has consequently lost an entire infinite cyclic interaction.

Reading the bilinear coefficient

To obtain a second derivative, Goodwillie linearizes the cross-effect separately in each input. In based spaces, linearization repeatedly suspends an input and compensates by looping the output; passing to the stable limit retains the part that responds linearly in that input. Doing this in both variables gives a bilinear response. This plays the role of extracting the coefficient of from the mixed difference, while keeping homotopical information instead of a scalar.

For the identity, the resulting calculation is

The dimension count makes the loop shift intelligible. Suspending the two sphere inputs and times changes their dimensions to and . The product cell then has dimension , and its attaching boundary has dimension . Compensating with output loops restores degree three. The full bilinear equivalence above is Goodwillie's theorem; the cell calculation explains why its coefficient has a one-degree desuspension.

For based CW models, the smash product retains the part of the product that requires both inputs. At , it is . Thus

We can track the specific Whitehead class through the comparison, rather than only compare the groups. Put and . The quotient sends the wedge to the basepoint and induces

A point of the fiber includes a path in from its wedge image to the basepoint; quotienting this path gives a based loop in . The second arrow is stabilization. The characteristic product four-cell represents a generator of , and its boundary is the chosen mixed Whitehead map. After quotienting by the wedge, this cell gives a degree-one map

Its fiber lift therefore maps to a generator, up to the orientation sign, of . The bilinear response detects this mixed class with its chosen nullhomotopy. The maps and extensions assembling the Taylor stages still require further data.

The one-loop shift also explains the coefficient spectrum: the second derivative is the desuspended sphere with trivial transposition action,

where the subscript denotes homotopy orbits. The trivial action belongs to the coefficient sphere; transposition still exchanges the two inputs. Writing and , the relevant expansion is

The two middle terms are the ordered mixed choices. Transposition exchanges that pair. After smashing with the coefficient , their homotopy orbits leave exactly one copy of . Applying gives the bilinear term above. This identification accounts for the exchange of inputs through the homotopy structure, rather than division by a numerical factorial.

For simply connected spaces, including , the identity's tower converges to the original space. Reconstruction uses the maps and extensions connecting the layers, as well as their derivative spectra. The sequence of coefficients alone does not determine how the layers assemble.

These are derivatives of a functor between homotopy theories. Their variables are spaces, and their changes are gluing operations. The connection with the rectangle is precise at that level: isolate simultaneous interaction, extract its bilinear part, and specify what the linear approximation discarded. It does not identify these spectra with derivatives of point coordinates.

14 · What differentiation retains and what reconstruction requires

The rectangle's two strips give the elementary result: first-order multiplication changes one factor at a time. The corner is a simultaneous change of both factors. The Leibniz rule is the compatibility condition that remains when products of changes are discarded. The oriented boundary adds another requirement: retain degrees and signs so that contributions from adjoining pieces cancel compatibly. These two operations guided the algebraic quotients, the graded resolutions, and the product-cell attachments above.

Each subsequent construction makes the retained information more precise. Kähler differentials represent all first-order measurements compatible with an algebra. The cotangent complex retains equations and homological dependencies in those measurements. Higher jets retain powers of displacement, so they can distinguish a quadratic obstruction from a cubic one. Full formal deformation theory assembles infinitesimal probes of every order, together with their compatibility and homotopies.

The example shows why these distinctions matter. Equal pointwise tangent complexes can coexist with different formal neighborhoods. Higher brackets recover the equation because they specify how several tangent inputs combine into an obstruction. Spectral differentiation keeps coherent multiplication and spectral coefficients; Goodwillie differentiation keeps the interactions a functor creates when spaces are combined.

This gives a concrete reconstruction question in the Tensorgami spirit. Choose the probes and the representation of their responses. Determine which operations survive. Then identify the additional structure required to recover what was discarded. A derivative can be universal for first-order measurements while remaining incomplete as a description of the whole object. The successful reconstruction theorem names both the information retained and the hypotheses under which it suffices.

The ordinary coefficient is one instance of this architecture. It records the action on the displacement . More elaborate derivatives preserve more of the surrounding algebra, equations, or homotopy theory, while continuing to answer a recognizable question: how does the object respond to a controlled change?
